meta.regime: The question this file set yesterday got a clean answer and the market did not trade it cleanly. The October 28 minutes landed at 21:00 and the hawkish bloc behind Cook and Hammack is not narrow - almost all participants judged further increases in the target range would likely be appropriate, and a couple said an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting if inflation data were unfavourable. The dollar added 0.06% to 103.900. The 10-year fell two basis points to 5.06%, the Dow lost 561 points, Nvidia reversed a 2.7% gain to close down 2.89%, and gold, silver and copper all bounced overnight. The reason is the second half of the same minutes: staff highlighted the rapid growth of debt associated with the AI buildout, most participants said that growth has come through complex and opaque financing structures, and almost all discussed the scenario in which returns on AI investment disappoint. A hawkish Fed went into the front end and a credit-and-growth worry went into equities and the long end. Underneath that, Australia printed the worst labour report of the cycle and the cleanest single trade on the board is now AUD against NZD rather than anything against the dollar.

dailyRead: Yesterday this file said the October 28 minutes at 21:00 were the test of whether the dollar deserved a plus three, and that the thing to watch was how wide the hawkish bloc behind Cook and Hammack really was. It is wide. The minutes record that almost all participants judged further action to raise the target range would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks, that a couple said an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting if inflation data were unfavourable, and that some saw market-implied expectations of December and 2027 tightening as broadly consistent with their own views. The vote to hold at 3.75% to 4.00% was 10-2, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack both preferring a quarter-point rise. On that alone the dollar should have gapped. It added 0.06%, to 103.900. What stopped it is the other half of the same document: the staff highlighted the rapid growth of debt associated with the artificial intelligence buildout, most participants noted that this growth has taken place through complex and opaque financing structures, many pointed to lower AI-related equity valuations, and almost all discussed the risks of a scenario in which returns on AI investment turn out to be disappointing. That is a hawkish central bank telling you it is worried about the credit behind the thing holding up the index. So the front end repriced hawkish and the long end did not: the 10-year fell two basis points to 5.06%, the Dow closed 561 points lower at 50,198 with UnitedHealth the biggest drag, the S&P fell for a fifth straight session and slipped below its 200-day moving average, and Nvidia gave back a 2.7% gain to finish 2.89% down on the day it beat. Overnight that softened further: gold is 3,739.69 and plus 0.38% after Wednesday took it 3% lower to a 14-month low, silver is 45.566 and plus 1.09% after a 5% fall, copper is 5.6866 and plus 0.47% after losing nearly 6%, and YM has bounced 400 points off a 1-month low. The practical read is that the dollar trend is intact but the marginal buyer is tired, so this is the day to keep the dollar longs where the cross has no story of its own and take conviction down where it does. The cross that does have a story is the Australian dollar. October employment fell 43,500 against a plus 25,500 forecast and unemployment went to 4.9% from 4.7%, the highest in four years, and Moody’s said the print closes the door on a December hike. The trap is to read that as a currency you can simply sell, because Australian inflation is 4.3% and rising with core at 3.6%, the highest on the board, and the cash rate is 4.85%. The Reserve Bank cannot hike into 4.9% unemployment and cannot cut into 4.3% inflation, so the Australian dollar now has a central bank that is frozen rather than dovish. New Zealand is the exact mirror and almost nobody is framing it that way: inflation there is 3.7% and falling from 4.1%, and TradingEconomics still carries 3.00% for the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement with survey respondents at 3.05% by year end. One frozen bank against one still hiking is why AUD/NZD fell 0.61% to 1.21697 overnight, the largest cross move on the board, and why it is upgraded from range to a medium-conviction short while AUD/USD stays the high-conviction dollar expression. The kiwi itself gets an upgrade for an unglamorous reason: yesterday it was cut to minus two explicitly on price rather than policy, after breaking 55 US cents to a six-year low, and today the price leg stopped working - NZD/USD is 0.54958 and minus 0.02%, flat against a dollar at a 19-month high, and the kiwi gained on five of the other seven. That is the leg of the thesis that broke, so the score goes back to minus one. The yen is the other change. It had risen against all seven others for four straight sessions and that run ended overnight: USD/JPY is 159.544 and plus 0.12%, and the yen is lower against six of the eight, higher only against the Australian dollar. The haven bid faded with the metals bounce, which leaves the yen as a carry funder again rather than a safe asset, so it comes back from plus two to plus one. The forward case is untouched and still the strongest on the board after the dollar: 61 of 71 economists expect a quarter-point move to 1.50% on December 18, nearly 60% see 1.75% by the end of March, Japanese national core CPI tomorrow at 01:30 is forecast at 2.3% against 2.1%, and the Ministry of Finance has spent close to 100 billion dollars this year defending a currency that is 46 pips from 160. That is why USD/JPY stays a range and not a long: the Fed argues up, the Bank of Japan and the Ministry of Finance argue down, and 160 is where the second pair stops arguing and acts. Europe is the quiet hawkish story. Euro-area inflation is 4.0%, a three-year high, the deposit rate is 2.50% after the October 29 hold, December 17 is priced somewhere between 67% and 84%, and the energy leg that was supposed to be fading is firmly back: EU natural gas rose 1.73% to 82.11 euros. Lagarde said there would be many indicators between now and December to help determine whether a hike is necessary, and she speaks twice inside 20 hours, at 15:30 today and 10:15 tomorrow. None of that has rescued EUR/USD, which is 1.09655 and minus 0.12% in the 19-month low zone, so the euro stays a zero - but it is a zero that outperformed five of the seven others, and EUR/USD comes down from high conviction to medium because a short that fights both a hawkish ECB and rising European gas is no longer a free trade. Sterling is where the cleanest asymmetry in rate pricing sits. The Bank of England hiked to 4.00% on November 5, CPI is 3.6% with core steady at 2.8%, unemployment improved to 4.6%, and the market prices December 17 at 79% to 84% while 64 of 65 economists polled by Reuters expect a hold and Bailey declined to endorse the move at all. The gap between those two numbers is the trade and it points the same way as the short. Canada is unchanged and unambiguous: USD/CAD is 1.4340, the Canadian dollar is at a 19-month low, October core CPI fell to 2.0% with trimmed at 1.8% and median at 2.0%, unemployment is 6.7% and rising, December hike odds are down to 38%, and WTI at 83.29 is 14% lower on the month. Switzerland stays the second-choice haven with the policy rate at zero and inflation at 1.5% that is almost entirely energy, since core is 0.5%. For the Dow, the overnight bounce is real but counter-trend: YM is 50,491 and plus 0.43%, above yesterday’s close at 50,273 and above VWAP at 50,423, having based at a 1-month low of 50,096, with the week still down 3.96% and the index below a 200-day average the S&P already lost. Walmart reports before the open, there is no red folder in either session, and five Fed speakers are spread across the day starting with Hammack - a hiking dissenter - at 15:50. Not financial advice.

today.headline: October employment fell 43,500 against a plus 25,500 forecast and unemployment jumped to 4.9%, a four-year high - the worst labour print of the cycle.
today.read: AUD/USD 0.66911 and minus 0.56%, AUD/NZD minus 0.61%, AUD/CAD minus 0.33%, AUD/CHF minus 0.32%, weakest on the board and the score to minus three. TradingEconomics confirms both lines. The analytical point is that this does not make the Australian dollar a dovish-bank currency: inflation is 4.3% and rising with core at 3.6%, the highest here, against a 4.85% cash rate. A board that cannot hike into 4.9% unemployment and cannot cut into 4.3% inflation is frozen, and a frozen bank is worth less than a cutting one to a carry trade but more to a crisis hedge. Express it against New Zealand, where the bank is still expected to move, rather than only against a dollar that is already stretched.

today.read: DXY 103.900 and plus 0.06%, still the highest since April 2025. Keep the dollar at plus three on level and policy divergence, but treat 103.90 as a crowded trade rather than a fresh breakout, and let the crosses with their own stories carry the conviction. Five speakers today starting with Hammack, who dissented for a hike, at 15:50.

today.headline: Quiet after yesterday’s fall, with the December mispricing between the market at 79% to 84% and 64 of 65 economists expecting a hold still open.
today.read: GBP/USD 1.3135 and minus 0.10%, EUR/GBP 0.83469 and plus 0.03%, little changed on the crosses. The move happened yesterday when Bailey declined to endorse December and said policy is not on a pre-set path. The data is genuinely two-sided - CPI 3.6%, core steady at 2.8%, unemployment improved to 4.6% - and that is exactly why the swap market and the economist consensus have not converged. The trade is the gap, and it points down: if the economists are right the December premium comes out of sterling. Dhingra at 14:15 and retail sales tomorrow at 09:00 are the near-term inputs, neither of them large.

Nothing new today, and nothing needs to be: core CPI at 2.0% with trimmed at 1.8% and median at 2.0%, unemployment 6.7% and rising, a third consecutive monthly fall in employment, and WTI at 83.29 and down 14% on the month have taken away the reason for the October hike. USD/CAD stays the highest-conviction dollar long on the board precisely because it does not depend on the dollar leg doing any more work. IPPI and RMPI at 15:30 and retail sales tomorrow are both low-impact.

today.headline: Flat everywhere as the second-choice haven, with the franc neither bid by the metals bounce nor sold by it.
today.read: EUR/CHF 0.92518 and minus 0.04%, USD/CHF 0.84361 and plus 0.03%, GBP/CHF minus 0.09%, CAD/CHF minus 0.02%, NZD/CHF plus 0.08%, AUD/CHF minus 0.32%. Inflation at 1.5% looks like the highest in nearly three years until core at 0.5% shows it is imported energy, which is why the December 10 hold is not in question and the policy rate stays at zero. The franc’s role on this board is as the quiet alternative when the yen is doing the haven work; with the yen’s run over, that role is empty today. The constraint remains the SNB’s willingness to sell francs, which caps any rally before it starts.

USD.when: December 9 at 21:00 with a new dot plot, and the minutes widened rather than narrowed the hawkish bloc
USD.note: TradingEconomics carries the Fed funds rate at 4.00% for October as the upper bound of the 3.75% to 4.00% range, held on October 28 by 10-2 with Cook and Hammack dissenting for a quarter-point rise. The October 28 minutes published last night record that almost all participants judged further action to raise the target range would likely be appropriate, that a couple said an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting if inflation data were unfavourable, and that some saw market pricing for December and 2027 as broadly consistent with their own views. CME-based measures put December between 90% and 95.7% for a quarter point with the fifty-point tail between 4% and 10%. The meeting is one of four a year carrying a Summary of Economic Projections, so the dot plot is the bigger half of the event.

EUR.when: December 17 at 15:15, priced between 67% and 84%, and the energy leg is back in the ECB’s favour
EUR.note: TradingEconomics carries the deposit facility rate at 2.50% with the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%, all held on October 29. Euro-area inflation is 4.0%, a three-year high, with core at 2.6% and rising. Lagarde said there would be many indicators between now and December to help determine whether a hike is necessary, which leaves the decision open rather than committed, and she speaks at 15:30 today and 10:15 tomorrow. EU natural gas rose 1.73% to 82.11 euros, so the input that drove the 4.0% print is strengthening rather than fading. The meeting accounts for October land on November 26. Lagarde has said she steps down on February 7, 2027, which starts to matter for the 2027 path rather than this one.

GBP.when: December 17 at 14:00, where the market says 79% to 84% and 64 of 65 economists say hold
GBP.note: TradingEconomics carries Bank Rate at 4.00% after the November 5 quarter-point rise from 3.75%. CPI is 3.6% with core steady at 2.8%, and unemployment improved to 4.6% from 4.7% although the ONS has flagged Labour Force Survey sample rotation behind part of that. The gap between overnight index swap pricing near 84% and a Reuters poll in which 64 of 65 economists expect no move is the widest mispricing on this board, and Bailey widened it himself by declining to endorse December and saying policy is not on a pre-set path. Oxford Economics expects 4.25% at either the December or the February meeting. Dhingra speaks at 14:15 today.

JPY.when: December 18 at 05:00 or earlier, with 61 of 71 economists expecting 1.50%
JPY.note: TradingEconomics carries the policy rate at 1.25% after the October 30 hold, following the September 18 rise from 1.00%. A Reuters poll has 61 of 71 economists, about 86%, expecting a quarter-point move to 1.50% on December 17 to 18, which would make this the first three-hike year in 37 years, and nearly 60% expect 1.75% by the end of March. Ueda has said he expects to keep raising rates and warned inflation could overshoot the 2% target. National core CPI tomorrow at 01:30 is forecast at 2.3% against 2.1% and would effectively lock the move. The nearer risk is not the Bank but the Ministry of Finance: close to 100 billion dollars has gone into defending the yen this year, Mimura has warned against excessive volatility, and spot is 159.544.

AUD.when: December 8 at 05:30, and after this morning the hold is not in question - the peak is
AUD.note: TradingEconomics carries the cash rate at 4.85% after the November 3 rise from 4.60%, the second hike in three meetings. This morning removed the December question: employment fell 43,500 against a plus 25,500 forecast and unemployment rose to 4.9% from 4.7%, the highest in four years, and Moody’s said the print closes the door on a December hike. What it does not do is open a cut, because headline inflation is 4.3% and rising with core at 3.6%, the highest on the board. That leaves a board that can neither tighten into a deteriorating labour market nor ease into accelerating prices, so the path is a flat 4.85% with the debate shifting to whether this is the peak. November labour data is due December 17.

NZD.when: December 9 at 03:00, the only bank on the board expected to tighten into falling inflation
NZD.note: TradingEconomics carries the official cash rate at 2.75% after the October 28 hold, and still forecasts 3.00% for the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement, with survey respondents putting the rate at 3.05% by the end of December. Inflation is 3.7% and falling from 4.1%, core is 3.2%, and the November 17 inflation expectations survey put the two-year measure at 2.36% and the one-year at 2.92%. Unemployment at 5.7% is the counter-argument and the reason the hike is not fully owned. The distinction that matters for crosses is that this is the one currency here whose central bank is expected to raise rates while its inflation rate is coming down, which is the opposite of Australia.

CAD.when: December 9 at 16:45, with hike odds down to 38% from 54% before the October CPI
CAD.note: TradingEconomics carries the overnight rate at 2.50% after the October 28 rise from 2.25%, the first move of the cycle. October CPI then undercut the reason for it: headline held at 3.1% against a 3.2% forecast, core fell to 2.0% from 2.2%, trimmed came in at 1.8% and median at 2.0%, so both preferred measures sit at or below the midpoint of the target band. Unemployment is 6.7% and rising, employment fell for a third consecutive month, and the energy spillover the bank hiked to pre-empt is unwinding with WTI down 14% on the month to 83.29. Implied December odds are 38%, CIBC and KPMG expect a hold and only Oxford Economics still looks for a move. The Monetary Policy Report comes on January 27.

CHF.when: December 10 at 10:30, where a hold is as close to certain as anything on this board
CHF.note: TradingEconomics carries the SNB policy rate at 0.00%, held at every one of the March 19, June 18 and September 24 decisions. Inflation is 1.5%, close to a three-year high, but core is 0.5%, which says the move is almost entirely imported energy and not something the bank needs to respond to. Unemployment is stable at 3.0% and wage growth is 0.4%. The bank’s active instrument remains the exchange rate rather than the rate itself, and its readiness to sell francs is the thing that caps any haven rally, with EUR/CHF at 0.92518 and USD/CHF at 0.84361. The next scheduled decision after December 10 is March 18.

symbols.why: 174.968 and plus 0.06%, a zero against a plus one, so the smallest edge in the book. Two hawkish banks mostly cancel.

symbols.why: 1.63911 and plus 0.33%, a zero against a minus three, and one of the two best-performing crosses overnight. symbols.why: 0.83469 and plus 0.03%, a zero against a minus one. The gap resolves in the euro’s favour if the economists are right.

symbols.why: 1.5720 and plus 0.01%, a zero against a minus two. WTI up through 95 would support the Canadian dollar through terms of trade while raising European gas costs in a way that hurts growth more than it helps the hawks. symbols.why: 0.92518 and minus 0.04%, a zero against a zero, which is as flat as a cross gets. symbols.why: 1.96316 and plus 0.32%, a minus one against a minus three, and one of the better-performing crosses overnight. symbols.why: 2.38962 and minus 0.18%, a minus one against a minus one after the kiwi upgrade, so the score edge that justified a long has gone. symbols.why: 1.10826 and minus 0.09%, a minus one against a zero. symbols.why: 0.56441 and minus 0.32%, a minus three against a zero. symbols.why: 0.78800 and plus 0.11%, a minus one against a minus two, moving from range on equal scores to a long after the kiwi upgrade. symbols.why: 0.46373 and plus 0.08%, a minus one against a zero, so the smallest edge there is and the price moved against it overnight. The kiwi was the second-best performer on the board and its central bank is still expected to tighten on December 9, which is poor material for a short.

This is a hold-nothing entry until either leg produces a reason, and the same view is better taken in AUD/CHF.

symbols.why: 0.58854 and minus 0.02%, a minus two against a zero. symbols.why: 189.120 and plus 0.09%, a zero against a plus one. The case rests entirely on the Bank of Japan: 61 of 71 economists expect 1.50% on December 18 and national core CPI tomorrow at 01:30 is forecast at 2.3% from 2.1%, against a Swiss National Bank that will hold at zero on December 10.

A soft Japanese core CPI tomorrow removes the only real leg. Both currencies are havens, so a Hormuz escalation is close to neutral here.

symbols.why: 103.900 and plus 0.06%, the highest since April 2025, with all four components weak - euro 57.6%, yen 13.6%, sterling 11.9% and Canadian dollar 9.1%. The October minutes put almost all participants behind further hikes and a couple behind more than 25 basis points in December, which is priced 90% to 95.7%.

The 10-year fell two basis points to 5.06% on a hawkish day and the AI-credit passage in the same minutes gave the long end a counterweight, which is why this is medium rather than high. US jobless claims at 15:30 are the near-term squeeze risk.

symbols.why: The basket rises when the yen strengthens and the yen is now MIXED rather than STRENGTHENING, so this goes from long to range. The four-session run against all seven others ended overnight: the yen is lower against six of the eight and higher only against the Australian dollar, as the haven bid left with the metals bounce.
symbols.risk: This is the opposite ticket to the XXX/JPY pairs, so it inherits the same binary - Japanese national core CPI tomorrow at 01:30, forecast 2.3% against 2.1%. An upside print restores the long. The Ministry of Finance near 160 is the other upside trigger, having spent close to 100 billion dollars this year.

symbols.why: 25,822.6 and plus 0.31%, about 4.4% below the all-time high of 27,011 set this month. symbols.why: 6,181.6 and plus 0.48%, about 6.1% below the August all-time high of 6,582.30, and scored on its own evidence rather than the DAX’s. The leg dominating today is banks: Deutsche Bank has lost 10% since the start of the week on whistleblower file leaks, and banks are the index’s heaviest sector. The offset is semiconductors, with ASML up 2%.
symbols.risk: A rising curve and a hawkish European Central Bank normally help the bank weight, but a legal and governance story overrides the curve for the sector’s largest name, so the usual hawkish-ECB tailwind is not available this week. French and Italian political risk, which the DAX does not carry, is the other asymmetry. Lagarde at 15:30.

symbols.why: 3,739.69 and plus 0.38% after Wednesday took it 3% lower to a 14-month low near 3,736, the weakest since September 2025. The real-rate case is intact with the 10-year at 5.06% against 3.7% CPI and almost all FOMC participants wanting more hikes, but the bounce is the reason this comes down from high conviction.
symbols.risk: A 3% single-session capitulation into a 14-month low is where short-term shorts get squeezed, and the 10-year actually fell two basis points on the hawkish minutes. The AI-credit warning in those same minutes is the genuine bull case for gold, because a credit scare is the one thing that beats a high real rate.

symbols.why: 45.566 and plus 1.09% after a 5% fall to about 44.88 on Wednesday. Same real-rate driver as gold and the same downgrade from high conviction, but with a larger bounce - silver outperformed gold overnight, which is the industrial leg reasserting itself after copper also recovered 0.47%.
symbols.risk: Silver’s industrial demand leg can decouple it from gold in both directions, and it is the more violent of the two on squeezes - a 5% down day followed by a 1.09% bounce is the warning. If the AI-capex worry in the minutes develops into a genuine credit event, the industrial leg turns from support into the main downside driver.

symbols.why: 5.6866 dollars a pound and plus 0.47% after losing nearly 6% on Wednesday on AI-investment doubts, Chinese demand concerns and US trade policy. The Australian link is doing the work: Australia just printed a four-year-high unemployment rate of 4.9% with employment down 43,500, and copper and the Australian dollar trade the same China cycle.
symbols.risk: The AI-capex story cuts both ways - the FOMC minutes flagged opaque AI-related debt, but the physical buildout is also a real source of copper demand, so a reassuring Anthropic debut or AI headline can bid it. Chinese PMIs and any mine disruption are the supply-side risks to a short at these levels.

symbols.why: 83.2866 and minus 0.07%, down 14% on the month, with Brent at 92.2103 and plus 0.24%. Moved from short to range: the strait is closed on day 263 with Iran claiming a fourth tanker struck in 24 hours and Kpler putting flows at about 48% of pre-war levels, and the market will not bid any of it. A premium that is already gone cannot unwind further.
symbols.risk: The asymmetry is now upside and the trend is still down, which is what range means here. A market that discounts live escalation has nothing left priced for a real supply event, so the gap risk above is larger than the drift below. Kept consistent with a weak Canadian dollar: a firm-crude thesis would require the Canadian read to change first.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz closure, day 263, and the absent crude premium
catalysts.note: Iran claims a fourth oil tanker struck in 24 hours and UKMTO reported a vessel hit by an unknown projectile with a resulting engine-room fire, while the United States enforces a naval blockade of Iran’s Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports and Iran claims control of the strait. Transit counts are estimates and conflict sharply: one tracker reports a single tanker transit on its latest complete day against a pre-crisis baseline near 85 transits daily. Kpler’s estimate of about 8.3 million barrels a day in the week to November 11, roughly 48% of the 17.1 million pre-war level, remains the most useful single figure and is preliminary. WTI is 83.29 and down 14% on the month regardless. Iranian casualty tallies are unverified and Iranian state media has reported differing totals.

geopolitics: The transmission has now fully inverted and it is worth stating plainly, because it is the single most important thing on this board that nobody is paid to say: the news is getting worse and the price is going down, and that is information rather than noise. Day 263 of the closure. Iran’s armed forces claim a fourth oil tanker struck in 24 hours, UKMTO reported a vessel hit by an unknown projectile with a resulting engine-room fire, the United States says it is enforcing a naval blockade of Iran’s Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports while Iran claims control of the strait itself, and Trump has publicly raised Iranian gases and biological weapons alongside a dirty-bomb report. The physical numbers remain estimates rather than data and should be treated that way: one tracker reports a single tanker transit on its most recent complete UTC day and two ships on November 15 against a pre-crisis baseline near 85 transits a day, Iranian state media has published differing totals for tanker casualties, and no maritime authority has independently confirmed the Iranian count. Kpler remains the most useful single figure - about 8.3 million barrels a day in the week to November 11, roughly 48% of the 17.1 million pre-war level, and preliminary. Against all of that, WTI is 83.2866 and minus 0.07%, down 14% on the month, and Brent is 92.2103 and plus 0.24%, with one tracker quoting Brent as low as 90.87. A market that will not bid live escalation is a market with no remaining premium to unwind, and the practical consequence is that the direction of the asymmetry has flipped even though the direction of the trend has not. That is exactly why USOIL moves from a short to a range today rather than staying with the trend: the downside is drift and the upside is a gap. The FX read follows from the same inversion. The Canadian dollar has been the main casualty and stays a minus two: the Bank of Canada hiked in October specifically to stop energy spreading into other goods, and energy has since fallen 14% while core CPI dropped to 2.0%, trimmed to 1.8% and median to 2.0% - the stated reason for the hike has been removed by the bank’s own data, December odds are 38%, and USD/CAD at 1.4340 is a 19-month low for the currency. Europe is the mirror image and this is where the reversal actually bites, because the crude move and the gas move have separated: EU natural gas rose 1.73% to 82.11 euros while crude fell, so the euro-area keeps the inflation cost of the conflict without the terms-of-trade relief, which is precisely the mechanism holding euro-area inflation at a three-year high of 4.0% and keeping the December 17 hike priced at 67% to 84%. That split is also why GER40 and EU50 both score as ranges rather than directional shorts: falling crude helps industrial margins while rising gas hurts them, and the two legs are currently cancelling. For the havens, the honest observation is that the conflict is no longer generating a haven bid at all - the yen’s four-session run against all seven others ended overnight on a day the tanker headlines got worse, and the franc was flat on every single cross. Both were bid by the Federal Reserve and by the metals rout, not by Hormuz, which is the clearest possible evidence that this market has stopped treating the strait as a tradeable risk. Keep the CHF crosses consistent with that: a zero score, no haven premium, and a Swiss National Bank at zero that will sell francs if one ever appears. The scenario that re-prices everything at once is a genuine supply interruption rather than another unconfirmed claim - WTI through 95 would restore the Canadian inflation argument and terms of trade together, invert the USD/CAD long, and force the European growth-versus-inflation trade-off back to the growth side. Nothing in the current price is paying for that.
